query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating targeted alloying elements such as Co and Ni into high-strength steels promotes the in situ formation of a self-enriching, protective surface film during service, thereby significantly reducing corrosion rates in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard high-strength steels without enhanced levels of Co and Ni, exhibiting conventional corrosion behavior in corrosive aqueous environments.
generation.intervention: Modify the steel composition to include elevated amounts of Co and Ni to enable redox-driven surface enrichment under corrosive conditions.
generation.conditions: Expose both modified and unmodified steels to controlled corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications (e.g., chloride-rich aqueous solutions at moderate temperatures and pH typical of these settings).
generation.structural_mediator: Selective diffusion and redistribution of Co and Ni atoms in the near-surface region that form a stable, compact passive film.
generation.mechanism: Under corrosive attack, dissolved Co2+ and Ni2+ ions are reduced at the surface via redox reactions, leading to their localized enrichment. This self-enriched passive film acts as a barrier that impedes further oxidation and reduces the dissolution rate of less noble elements, thereby enhancing overall corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steels with the Co and Ni modifications will display measurable enrichment of these elements in the near-surface region and exhibit significantly lower corrosion rates compared to unmodified steels under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: Unmodified high-strength steels that do not form a protective self-enriching film and thus show higher corrosion rates when exposed to the same corrosive environments.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in environments with moderate chloride concentrations and temperatures that mimic chemical processing and nuclear reactor conditions; its effectiveness may vary under extreme or non-standard environmental conditions where different corrosion mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The exact compositional thresholds for optimal surface enrichment and the quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance remain to be determined experimentally. Additionally, potential interactions with other alloying elements in complex steel matrices may influence performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-strength steel samples: one standard (control) and one modified with elevated Co and Ni. Subject both sets to identical corrosive testing in a chloride-rich aqueous solution at temperatures and pH values relevant to chemical-processing or nuclear-power applications. After a fixed exposure period, perform surface analyses and corrosion rate measurements.
measurements: Surface elemental composition (using XPS or EDS) to detect Co/Ni enrichment
Electrochemical corrosion assessments (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Surface film characterization (using SEM/TEM for film thickness and uniformity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified steels do not show statistically significant Co and Ni enrichment at the surface and do not exhibit a reduced corrosion rate compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Figure 6a,c shows that there is enrichment of Co and Ni (and to some degree Fe) in the near-surface region even more than the bulk alloy, suggesting that Co, Ni, and Fe may be enriched in the Al and Cr depleted regions. Ni2+, Co2+, and Fe2+ ions were reduced to atomic Ni, Co, and Fe at the surface and their diffusion was likely assisted by vacancies created during depletion of Al and Cr. However, similar effects were not observed in case of DS2205 duplex steel, possibly because of the lack of stable redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. In addition, there was significant depletion of the refractory element Mo from DS2205, as shown in Figure 6b,d. Figure 7 shows relatively high ΔG° for MoCl2, so depletion of Mo due to chloride formation is not expected. Hence, depletion of Mo in DS2205 may be caused by direct reaction with moisture and oxide impurities, resulting in the formation of unstable or volatile metallic oxides as follows []:

The corrosion behavior of dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (EHEA) and duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205) was studied in NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 molten salt at 450 °C and 650 °C. AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA showed superior molten salt corrosion resistance than DS2205, which was attributed to the following: (i)Higher Ni content in EHEA and sacrificial role of Al in reducing outward diffusion of Cr, Fe, and Ni in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and the different reactivity of formation of chlorides, as well as enrichment of Co and Ni in the corrosion layer.(ii)Thermodynamically driven corrosion between alloying elements and molten salt constituents or impurities present within the melt. Metallic impurities such as Ni2+, Fe2+, and Co2+ enhance the corrosion resistance of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 via enrichment of impurity ions such as Ni, Co, and Fe (to lesser extent) in the corrosion layer as temperature increases.(iii)A lower volume fraction of the BCC phase, which makes it less prone to galvanic corrosion. The phase-specific work function for the as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and DS2205 suggested micro-galvanic corrosion, with nobler L12 and FCC phase in EHEA and DS 2205, respectively, compared to the B2 and BCC phases.

reading.lever: Incorporate alloying elements that promote the formation of a protective, self-enriching surface film.
reading.why: Modifying the alloy composition to encourage beneficial elemental redistribution (e.g., enrichment of Co/Ni) has been shown to enhance corrosion resistance in harsh environments and is promising for steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
